6) Repeat (5) with $\sigma = 40$.

## Notation

Write the penalized RKHS component as \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\), and write the full fitted regression function as  
\[
m(x)=b_0+b_1x+g(x).
\]
The problem’s \(\hat f\) in later parts is therefore the full fitted function \(\hat m\).

Let

\[
Y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)^T,\qquad 
Z=\begin{pmatrix}
1&X_1\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
1&X_n
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
b=(b_0,b_1)^T,
\]
and let \(K\) be the Gaussian kernel Gram matrix
\[
K_{ij}=K_\sigma(X_i,X_j)=\exp\left\{-\frac{(X_i-X_j)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}.
\]
Also define
\[
\eta=n\lambda,\qquad A=K+\eta I_n.
\]

Assume \(Z\) has full column rank, i.e. the \(X_i\)’s are not all identical. If not, one should drop the redundant column or use a generalized inverse.

---

# 1) Representer form

For fixed \(b_0,b_1\), minimize over \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\)
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\{Y_i-b_0-b_1X_i-g(X_i)\}^2+\lambda\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2.
\]

Let
\[
\mathcal H_n=\operatorname{span}\{K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot):i=1,\dots,n\}.
\]
For any \(g\in\mathcal H_\sigma\), decompose orthogonally as
\[
g=g_\parallel+g_\perp,
\qquad 
g_\parallel\in\mathcal H_n,\quad g_\perp\perp\mathcal H_n.
\]
By the reproducing property,
\[
g_\perp(X_i)=\langle g_\perp,K_\sigma(X_i,\cdot)\rangle_{\mathcal H_\sigma}=0.
\]
Therefore the residual sum of squares depends only on \(g_\parallel\), while
\[
\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\|g_\parallel\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2+\|g_\perp\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
\ge \|g_\parallel\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2.
\]
Since \(\lambda>0\), any minimizer must have \(g_\perp=0\). Hence the penalized component has the representer form
\[
\hat g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i K_\sigma(X_i,x).
\]

Thus the full fitted function can be written as
\[
\boxed{
\hat m(x)=\hat b_0+\hat b_1x+\sum_{i=1}^n \hat c_i K_\sigma(X_i,x)
}
\]
with coefficients independent of the evaluation point \(x\).

This is the representer theorem applied with an unpenalized linear part.

---

# 2) Penalty and closed form for \((\hat b,\hat c)\)

If
\[
g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_iK_\sigma(X_i,x),
\]
then by the reproducing property,
\[
\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2
=
\sum_{i,j=1}^n c_ic_jK_\sigma(X_i,X_j)
=
c^TKc.
\]
Therefore the finite-dimensional criterion is
\[
Q(b,c)
=
\frac1n\|Y-Zb-Kc\|_2^2+\lambda c^TKc.
\]
Equivalently, multiplying by \(n\),
\[
\|Y-Zb-Kc\|_2^2+\eta c^TKc,
\qquad \eta=n\lambda.
\]

Let
\[
r=Y-Zb-Kc.
\]
The first-order condition with respect to the RKHS component gives
\[
\hat g=\frac1{n\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^n r_iK_\sigma(X_i,\cdot).
\]
Thus we may take
\[
c=\frac{r}{n\lambda}=\frac r\eta,
\]
so that
\[
r=\eta c.
\]
Since
\[
r=Y-Zb-Kc,
\]
we get
\[
Y-Zb-Kc=\eta c,
\]
or
\[
(K+\eta I)c+Zb=Y.
\]
The first-order condition with respect to \(b\) gives
\[
Z^Tr=0.
\]
Since \(r=\eta c\), this is equivalent to
\[
Z^Tc=0.
\]

Therefore \((\hat c,\hat b)\) solves the block system
\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
K+\eta I & Z\\
Z^T & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat c\\
\hat b
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
Y\\
0
\end{pmatrix}.
}
\]

Let
\[
A=K+\eta I,\qquad G=Z^TA^{-1}Z.
\]
Since \(A\succ0\) and \(Z\) has full column rank, \(G\succ0\). From
\[
A\hat c+Z\hat b=Y,
\]
we have
\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(Y-Z\hat b).
\]
Using \(Z^T\hat c=0\),
\[
Z^TA^{-1}(Y-Z\hat b)=0.
\]
Hence
\[
G\hat b=Z^TA^{-1}Y.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
\hat b=(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1}Y.
}
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
\hat c=A^{-1}(Y-Z\hat b).
}
\]

Equivalently, defining
\[
P_A=Z(Z^TA^{-1}Z)^{-1}Z^TA^{-1},
\]
we have
\[
\boxed{
\hat c=A^{-1}(I-P_A)Y.
}
\]

---

# 3) Linear smoother matrix \(S\)

The fitted values at the observed covariates are
\[
\hat{\mathbf f}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\hat m(X_1)\\
\vdots\\
\hat m(X_n)
\end{pmatrix}
=
Z\hat b+K\hat c.
\]

Using the formulas above,
\[
Z\hat b=P_AY,
\]
and
\[
\hat c=A^{-1}(I-P_A)Y.
\]
Therefore
\[
\hat{\mathbf f}
=
P_AY+KA^{-1}(I-P_A)Y.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
\hat{\mathbf f}=SY
}
\]
where
\[
\boxed{
S=P_A+KA^{-1}(I-P_A).
}
\]
Equivalently, since \(K=A-\eta I\),
\[
KA^{-1}=I-\eta A^{-1},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{
S=I-\eta A^{-1}(I-P_A).
}
\]

The matrix \(S\) depends on \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), \(\sigma\), and \(\lambda\), but not on \(Y\). Hence this is a linear smoother.

The effective degrees of freedom are
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{df}=\operatorname{tr}(S).
}
\]

---

# 4) R implementation

```r
partial.rkhs <- function(x, y, sigma, lambda, xnew = NULL, return.S = TRUE) {
  stopifnot(sigma > 0, lambda > 0)
  
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  y <- as.numeric(y)
  keep <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  x <- x[keep]
  y <- y[keep]
  
  n <- length(y)
  Z <- cbind(1, x)
  colnames(Z) <- c("(Intercept)", "x")
  
  if (qr(Z)$rank < 2) {
    stop("Design matrix [1, x] is not full rank.")
  }
  
  # Kernel matrix
  D <- outer(x, x, "-")
  K <- exp(-(D^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
  
  eta <- n * lambda
  A <- K + eta * diag(n)
  
  # Inverses/solves
  Ainv <- solve(A, diag(n))
  AinvZ <- Ainv %*% Z
  Ainvy <- Ainv %*% y
  
  G <- crossprod(Z, AinvZ)  # Z^T A^{-1} Z
  
  b <- drop(solve(G, crossprod(Z, Ainvy)))
  names(b) <- c("b0", "b1")
  
  ccoef <- drop(Ainvy - AinvZ %*% b)
  
  fitted <- drop(Z %*% b + K %*% ccoef)
  
  # Smoother matrix
  # P_A = Z (Z^T A^{-1} Z)^{-1} Z^T A^{-1}
  P <- Z %*% solve(G, t(AinvZ))
  Sfull <- P + K %*% Ainv %*% (diag(n) - P)
  df <- sum(diag(Sfull))
  
  # Prediction at new x-values
  pred <- NULL
  if (!is.null(xnew)) {
    xnew <- as.numeric(xnew)
    Znew <- cbind(1, xnew)
    Dnew <- outer(xnew, x, "-")
    Knew <- exp(-(Dnew^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
    pred <- drop(Znew %*% b + Knew %*% ccoef)
  }
  
  list(
    b = b,
    c = ccoef,
    fitted = fitted,
    pred = pred,
    df = df,
    S = if (return.S) Sfull else NULL,
    x = x,
    y = y,
    sigma = sigma,
    lambda = lambda
  )
}
```

A helper to choose \(\lambda\) for a target degrees of freedom:

```r
lambda.for.df <- function(x, y, sigma, target.df, lo = -30, hi = 30) {
  f <- function(loglam) {
    fit <- partial.rkhs(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      lambda = exp(loglam),
      return.S = FALSE
    )
    fit$df - target.df
  }
  
  flo <- f(lo)
  fhi <- f(hi)
  
  iter <- 0
  while (flo < 0 && iter < 50) {
    lo <- lo - 5
    flo <- f(lo)
    iter <- iter + 1
  }
  
  iter <- 0
  while (fhi > 0 && iter < 50) {
    hi <- hi + 5
    fhi <- f(hi)
    iter <- iter + 1
  }
  
  if (flo * fhi > 0) {
    stop("Target df not bracketed. It may be unattainable.")
  }
  
  exp(uniroot(f, c(lo, hi), tol = 1e-7)$root)
}
```

# 5) Ozone analysis with \(\sigma=10\)

The dataset file `LAozone.data` was not provided, so numerical values and plots cannot be produced here without fabricating results. The following is the exact analysis I would perform.

```r
ozone.analysis <- function(file = "LAozone.data", sigma) {
  dat <- read.table(file, header = TRUE)
  
  dat <- na.omit(dat[, c("dpg", "ozone")])
  x <- dat$dpg
  y <- dat$ozone
  
  target.dfs <- c(4, 6, 8, 12)
  grid <- seq(-80, 120, length.out = 500)
  
  cols <- c("dodgerblue3", "firebrick2", "darkgreen", "purple")
  
  plot(
    x, y,
    pch = 16,
    col = adjustcolor("gray30", alpha.f = 0.6),
    xlab = "dpg",
    ylab = "ozone",
    xlim = c(-80, 120),
    main = paste0("Partial RKHS fits, sigma = ", sigma)
  )
  
  fits <- vector("list", length(target.dfs))
  names(fits) <- paste0("df", target.dfs)
  
  lambdas <- numeric(length(target.dfs))
  achieved.df <- numeric(length(target.dfs))
  
  for (j in seq_along(target.dfs)) {
    lambdas[j] <- lambda.for.df(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      target.df = target.dfs[j]
    )
    
    fits[[j]] <- partial.rkhs(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      lambda = lambdas[j],
      xnew = grid,
      return.S = FALSE
    )
    
    achieved.df[j] <- fits[[j]]$df
    
    lines(
      grid,
      fits[[j]]$pred,
      col = cols[j],
      lwd = 2
    )
  }
  
  legend(
    "topright",
    legend = paste0(
      "df = ", target.dfs,
      ", lambda = ", signif(lambdas, 4)
    ),
    col = cols,
    lwd = 2,
    bty = "n"
  )
  
  summary.table <- data.frame(
    target.df = target.dfs,
    lambda = lambdas,
    achieved.df = achieved.df
  )
  
  print(summary.table)
  
  # Fitted values for df = 8 at the five smallest and largest dpg values
  fit8 <- fits[[which(target.dfs == 8)]]
  ord <- order(x)
  idx <- c(head(ord, 5), tail(ord, 5))
  
  table8 <- data.frame(
    group = c(rep("5 smallest dpg", 5), rep("5 largest dpg", 5)),
    dpg = x[idx],
    ozone = y[idx],
    fhat = fit8$fitted[idx]
  )
  
  print(table8)
  
  invisible(list(
    fits = fits,
    lambdas = lambdas,
    achieved.df = achieved.df,
    table8 = table8
  ))
}
```

To run the requested \(\sigma=10\) analysis:

```r
res10 <- ozone.analysis(file = "LAozone.data", sigma = 10)
```

This produces:

1. the four \(\lambda\)’s giving df \(4,6,8,12\);
2. a plot of the four fitted curves over `dpg` in \((-80,120)\);
3. the fitted values \(\hat f\) for df \(=8\) at the five smallest and five largest observed `dpg` values.

Because the dataset was not supplied, the actual numerical table cannot be reported here.

---

# 6) Ozone analysis with \(\sigma=40\)

The analysis is identical, changing only \(\sigma\).

```r
res40 <- ozone.analysis(file = "LAozone.data", sigma = 40)
```

To display the \(\sigma=10\) and \(\sigma=40\) fits side-by-side:

```r
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

res10 <- ozone.analysis(file = "LAozone.data", sigma = 10)
res40 <- ozone.analysis(file = "LAozone.data", sigma = 40)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

For the same effective degrees of freedom, \(\sigma=10\) allows more localized variation, because the Gaussian kernel is narrower. With \(\sigma=40\), the kernel is wider, so the fitted functions are smoother over larger ranges of `dpg`. The \(\lambda\)’s needed to hit the same df values will generally differ substantially between the two choices of \(\sigma\).

# 4) R implementation

```r
partial.rkhs <- function(x, y, sigma, lambda, xnew = NULL, return.S = TRUE) {
  stopifnot(sigma > 0, lambda > 0)
  
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  y <- as.numeric(y)
  keep <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  x <- x[keep]
  y <- y[keep]
  
  n <- length(y)
  Z <- cbind(1, x)
  colnames(Z) <- c("(Intercept)", "x")
  
  if (qr(Z)$rank < 2) {
    stop("Design matrix [1, x] is not full rank.")
  }
  
  # Kernel matrix
  D <- outer(x, x, "-")
  K <- exp(-(D^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
  
  eta <- n * lambda
  A <- K + eta * diag(n)
  
  # Inverses/solves
  Ainv <- solve(A, diag(n))
  AinvZ <- Ainv %*% Z
  Ainvy <- Ainv %*% y
  
  G <- crossprod(Z, AinvZ)  # Z^T A^{-1} Z
  
  b <- drop(solve(G, crossprod(Z, Ainvy)))
  names(b) <- c("b0", "b1")
  
  ccoef <- drop(Ainvy - AinvZ %*% b)
  
  fitted <- drop(Z %*% b + K %*% ccoef)
  
  # Smoother matrix
  # P_A = Z (Z^T A^{-1} Z)^{-1} Z^T A^{-1}
  P <- Z %*% solve(G, t(AinvZ))
  Sfull <- P + K %*% Ainv %*% (diag(n) - P)
  df <- sum(diag(Sfull))
  
  # Prediction at new x-values
  pred <- NULL
  if (!is.null(xnew)) {
    xnew <- as.numeric(xnew)
    Znew <- cbind(1, xnew)
    Dnew <- outer(xnew, x, "-")
    Knew <- exp(-(Dnew^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
    pred <- drop(Znew %*% b + Knew %*% ccoef)
  }
  
  list(
    b = b,
    c = ccoef,
    fitted = fitted,
    pred = pred,
    df = df,
    S = if (return.S) Sfull else NULL,
    x = x,
    y = y,
    sigma = sigma,
    lambda = lambda
  )
}
```

A helper to choose \(\lambda\) for a target degrees of freedom:

```r
lambda.for.df <- function(x, y, sigma, target.df, lo = -30, hi = 30) {
  f <- function(loglam) {
    fit <- partial.rkhs(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      lambda = exp(loglam),
      return.S = FALSE
    )
    fit$df - target.df
  }
  
  flo <- f(lo)
  fhi <- f(hi)
  
  iter <- 0
  while (flo < 0 && iter < 50) {
    lo <- lo - 5
    flo <- f(lo)
    iter <- iter + 1
  }
  
  iter <- 0
  while (fhi > 0 && iter < 50) {
    hi <- hi + 5
    fhi <- f(hi)
    iter <- iter + 1
  }
  
  if (flo * fhi > 0) {
    stop("Target df not bracketed. It may be unattainable.")
  }
  
  exp(uniroot(f, c(lo, hi), tol = 1e-7)$root)
}
```

# 5) Ozone analysis with \(\sigma=10\)

The dataset file `LAozone.data` was not provided, so numerical values and plots cannot be produced here without fabricating results. The following is the exact analysis I would perform.

```r
ozone.analysis <- function(file = "LAozone.data", sigma) {
  dat <- read.table(file, header = TRUE)
  
  dat <- na.omit(dat[, c("dpg", "ozone")])
  x <- dat$dpg
  y <- dat$ozone
  
  target.dfs <- c(4, 6, 8, 12)
  grid <- seq(-80, 120, length.out = 500)
  
  cols <- c("dodgerblue3", "firebrick2", "darkgreen", "purple")
  
  plot(
    x, y,
    pch = 16,
    col = adjustcolor("gray30", alpha.f = 0.6),
    xlab = "dpg",
    ylab = "ozone",
    xlim = c(-80, 120),
    main = paste0("Partial RKHS fits, sigma = ", sigma)
  )
  
  fits <- vector("list", length(target.dfs))
  names(fits) <- paste0("df", target.dfs)
  
  lambdas <- numeric(length(target.dfs))
  achieved.df <- numeric(length(target.dfs))
  
  for (j in seq_along(target.dfs)) {
    lambdas[j] <- lambda.for.df(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      target.df = target.dfs[j]
    )
    
    fits[[j]] <- partial.rkhs(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      sigma = sigma,
      lambda = lambdas[j],
      xnew = grid,
      return.S = FALSE
    )
    
    achieved.df[j] <- fits[[j]]$df
    
    lines(
      grid,
      fits[[j]]$pred,
      col = cols[j],
      lwd = 2
    )
  }
  
  legend(
    "topright",
    legend = paste0(
      "df = ", target.dfs,
      ", lambda = ", signif(lambdas, 4)
    ),
    col = cols,
    lwd = 2,
    bty = "n"
  )
  
  summary.table <- data.frame(
    target.df = target.dfs,
    lambda = lambdas,
    achieved.df = achieved.df
  )
  
  print(summary.table)
  
  # Fitted values for df = 8 at the five smallest and largest dpg values
  fit8 <- fits[[which(target.dfs == 8)]]
  ord <- order(x)
  idx <- c(head(ord, 5), tail(ord, 5))
  
  table8 <- data.frame(
    group = c(rep("5 smallest dpg", 5), rep("5 largest dpg", 5)),
    dpg = x[idx],
    ozone = y[idx],
    fhat = fit8$fitted[idx]
  )
  
  print(table8)
  
  invisible(list(
    fits = fits,
    lambdas = lambdas,
    achieved.df = achieved.df,
    table8 = table8
  ))
}
```

To run the requested \(\sigma=10\) analysis:

```r
res10 <- ozone.analysis(file = "LAozone.data", sigma = 10)
```

This produces:

1. the four \(\lambda\)’s giving df \(4,6,8,12\);
2. a plot of the four fitted curves over `dpg` in \((-80,120)\);
3. the fitted values \(\hat f\) for df \(=8\) at the five smallest and five largest observed `dpg` values.

# 6) Ozone analysis with \(\sigma=40\)

The analysis is identical, changing only \(\sigma\).

```r
res40 <- ozone.analysis(file = "LAozone.data", sigma = 40)
```

To display the \(\sigma=10\) and \(\sigma=40\) fits side-by-side:

```r
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

res10 <- ozone.analysis(file = "LAozone.data", sigma = 10)
res40 <- ozone.analysis(file = "LAozone.data", sigma = 40)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

For the same effective degrees of freedom, \(\sigma=10\) allows more localized variation, because the Gaussian kernel is narrower. With \(\sigma=40\), the kernel is wider, so the fitted functions are smoother over larger ranges of `dpg`. The \(\lambda\)’s needed to hit the same df values will generally differ substantially between the two choices of \(\sigma\).
